question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

3.text:
Under Evans the thought that a is F is not a sui generis singular
thought. To think the thought Fa at all is to think of a under a mode
of presentation which is the concept F. To possess the concept F is to
possess it as a general, articulable and substitutable way of thinking
of objects.

Hence to think that a is F is to be able to think x is F in general
for x a variable ranging over the domain in which F is applicable.
The Generality Constraint is the requirement that a thinkable
particular application of a concept entails mastery of the concept as a
general concept: if you can think Fa you can think the schema Fx and
you can think it of any object which can be thought of in the same
mode of presentation. In particular you can detach the reference to a
and operate with F in isolation.

The closure under the universal quantifier is then free if you already
have quantificational competence. Mastery of the concept F together
with mastery of the universal quantifier just is mastery of the closed
schema ∀xFx as an intelligible thought. The constraint gives
intelligibility, not truth. You can understand the content of ∀xFx
and you can in principle make the same mode of presentation the
content of a universal thought, even though Fa does not entail and
does not entail the truth of ∀xFx. The singular thought is
understood only insofar as its conceptual component is already
general.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, not in the sense of being committed to or being able to entertain the content of the closed universal proposition ∀x Fx.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the modes of presentation under which a subject can think of an object, not a licence to universalise the predicate. On Evans' view if you can think the singular atomic thought Fa you must think of a under a mode of presentation that is in principle generalizable. In particular you must grasp F as a property you can apply to things in general, i.e. you must be able to appreciate the open schema Fx and to deploy F in other general thoughts of the subject, e.g. to think of a as G, to think Gx→Fx, etc. That is a requirement on the concept F and on the mode of presentation of a, not a requirement that you be able to entertain the specific quantified content that F holds of everything.

Being able to understand universal quantification is a syntactical/semantic competence with the operator ∀. It does not by itself give you the content of ∀x Fx. You can fully understand Fa in the sense of grasping the property F as applied to a particular object a under a generalizable mode of presentation, whilst lacking any competence with, or truth-conditional grasp of, the proposition that F holds of every x. In particular you may be unable to evaluate, entertain or assent to ∀x Fx, and Evans' constraint does not force you to. It forces you to be in a position to think of a and F in a way that allows the substitution of an arbitrary variable for the singular term, i.e. to grasp the schema Fx, not that you must be able to understand or believe the universal closure ∀x Fx. The constraint is about generalizability of thought, not about logical generalisation from an instance.

4.text:
Under Evans the point of the Generality Constraint is not that from a particular
instance you are committed to a particular universal belief, it is that the
thought Fa must be thinkable through a general concept F.

If you can think the singular thought
* a is F
you must possess F as a mode of presentation that can be applied to an
object in general. That is just the possession of the open thought

* x is F

with a free variable x, i.e. the capacity to substitute any singular term
that you can entertain for x and still think a F-thought. In that sense you
must have a grasp of F as a function from objects to truth values, and you
must be able to entertain the schema F x for an arbitrary x.

It is this open, generalizable schema that the Generality Constraint
demands. The closed quantified sentence

* ∀x Fx

is the schema F x closed with the universal quantifier. Possession of the
schema does not by itself entail possession of, nor endorsement of, the
closed quantified proposition ∀x Fx. You can understand the open sentence
F x and even understand what the universal quantifier does without being
in a position to assert or even to be able to evaluate the universal
generalisation ∀x Fx.

That is why the constraint is usually glossed as from Fa to the ability
to think F x for x arbitrary. If you in addition master the quantifier ∀
you can of course combine your grasp of F x with your grasp of ∀ and form
the sentence ∀x Fx in the object language, but the formation of the closed
universal is a further step that goes beyond the Generality Constraint
proper. In the conventional shorthand the possession of F x for an
arbitrary x is said to be possession of ∀x Fx, and on that shorthand the
answer is yes: a grasp of Fa requires a general grasp of F, i.e. a grasp
of the general form F x and, modulo your independent grasp of ∀, of the
sentential form ∀x Fx. Strictly speaking the constraint gives you the
open schema F x, not the inescapable endorsement of the universal
generalisation ∀x Fx.

2.text:
The generality constraint is a constraint on the thinker's cognitive
competence with the concept F, not a licence to pass from a singular
instance to a universal claim about the world.

On Evans' view to be able to think that a is F is to possess F as a
general concept of yours and to be able to redeploy it. If you can think
the thought that is expressed by

    Fa

that is Fa with a thought of a in a particular mode of presentation,
you must be able to think of a under that same mode of presentation
together with any other concept you possess, i.e. you must be able to
entertain the schema

    Fx

for an arbitrary object x, and in particular you must be able to
entertain Ga for every G you understand. That is the generalizability
which the constraint enforces: the mode of presentation of a in Fa must
be one which is available for arbitrary co-instantiation with predicates.
In that weak sense you must possess F as a predicate of variables, not
as an idiosyncratic property of a.

It does not follow from that that you must be able to understand, in
the sense of grasp the truth conditions of, the closed universal

    ∀x Fx

Understanding ∀x Fx is to understand the claim that every object falls
under F. The generality constraint gives you F as a general
conceptual role and, given independent competence with the quantifier,
the syntactic ability to form the expression ∀x Fx. It does not give
you an entitlement to the content that every x is F, nor does it make the
understanding of Fa depend on your having an opinion, true or false,
about all the Fs. Fa can be understood perfectly well while ∀x Fx is
understood as false, unknown, or even unconsidered. The constraint is
about the ability to think about a in general ways, i.e. to think Fx
for arbitrary x, and not about the truth of a universal generalisation
over F.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is whether, given Evans' Generality Constraint and assuming independent competence with ∀, understanding Fa requires being able to understand the closed universal proposition ∀x Fx, or only the open schema Fx.

Colleagues 1,2,4 converge on a negative / qualified answer: the constraint is about the mode of presentation / concept possession, not about entitlement to a universal claim. To think Fa you must think of a under a mode of presentation that is generalizable, i.e. you must possess F as a general concept and be able to entertain the open schema Fx and deploy F with other predicates, e.g. be able to think Ga for every G you understand, to think of a as F together with an arbitrary variable. That is generalizability of thought, not logical generalisation from an instance. Understanding ∀ is syntactic/semantic competence with the operator; it does not by itself give you the truth-conditional content of ∀x Fx. You can fully grasp Fa with a generalizable concept F while lacking any competence with, or while being agnostic/false about, the proposition ∀x Fx. The constraint gives the open schema Fx for arbitrary x, not inescapable endorsement of the closed quantified proposition. Formation of ∀x Fx is a further step beyond the constraint proper.

Colleague 3 dissents: to think Fa is to think of a under a mode of presentation which is the concept F. Possessing F is possessing it as general, articulable and substitutable. Hence to think Fa is to be able to think x is F in general for x a variable. With independent mastery of the quantifier, mastery of F together with mastery of ∀ just is mastery of the closed schema ∀x Fx as an intelligible thought. Intelligibility, not truth, is given; Fa does not entail truth of ∀x Fx but the conceptual component is already general, so the universal closure is free.

Key distinction preserved: open generalizable schema Fx vs closed quantified content ∀x Fx; intelligibility vs endorsement/truth-conditional grasp; generalizability of the mode of presentation vs licence to universalise.

Unresolved for me: whether Evans identifies the ability to entertain Fx for arbitrary x, given quantifier competence, with being able to understand/undertake the closed proposition ∀x Fx as an intelligible thought, or whether the constraint stops at the open schema. The split between Colleague 3's closure-is-free view and Colleagues 1,2,4's constraint-is-only-open view remains.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The debate is about what the Generality Constraint requires from understanding Fa: an open generalizable schema Fx for arbitrary x, or the closed quantified content ∀x Fx.

Common ground from Colleagues 1,2,4 and 3: On Evans, thinking Fa is not sui generis singular. To think Fa you must possess F as a general, articulable concept that can be redeployed with other concepts and with a variable. That is, you must be able to appreciate the open schema Fx and to think of a under a mode of presentation that is available for arbitrary co-instantiation. The constraint is a constraint on modes of presentation / conceptual competence, not a licence to infer the truth of a universal generalisation from an instance.

Division:
* Colleagues 1,2,4: Generality gives the open schema Fx, not the closed universal proposition ∀x Fx. Understanding universal quantification is a separate syntactic/semantic competence. Having F as general plus quantification competence gives you the ability to form the expression ∀x Fx, but the constraint does not force you to be able to entertain, evaluate or assent to the content that every x is F. You can understand Fa while ∀x Fx is unknown, false or unconsidered. In the conventional shorthand people conflate possession of Fx for arbitrary x with possession of ∀x Fx, strictly the constraint yields the open schema only.
* Colleague 3: Possession of F as general together with quantifier mastery just is mastery of the closed schema ∀x Fx as an intelligible thought. The singular thought is understood only insofar as its conceptual component is already general, so the universal closure is free once ∀ is understood. The constraint gives intelligibility, not truth, and Fa does not entail the truth of ∀x Fx.

Unresolved / important: the sense of 'understand'. If 'understand' = have an intelligible content/ability to entertain the thought, then with independent ∀ competence the closed universal becomes intelligible; if 'understand' = be committed to/able to assess the truth-conditions of ∀x Fx, the constraint does not require it. The key distinction remains open schema Fx for arbitrary x vs endorsement/ evaluation of ∀x Fx.

My current synthesis: Generality requires the open generalizability Fx. That plus independent mastery of ∀ makes ∀x Fx syntactically/formally intelligible, but Evans's constraint alone does not commit you to the truth or even to entertaining the universal proposition. The disagreement is largely terminological about whether to identify the open schema with the universal closure.
